claims.text: Applying a gradient, self-healing thermally adaptive coating to CoCrFeNi will induce in-situ formation and regeneration of a lubricious tribofilm during sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
The starting material is an unmodified, coarse-grained bulk CoCrFeNi alloy.
The engineered gradient coating will form a continuously regenerating lubricious tribofilm when exposed to friction and elevated temperature.
Frictional heat and mechanical stress will cause the coating to develop a nanocrystalline glaze layer or comparable lubricious phase.
The resulting glaze or lubricious phase will lower interfacial shear strength.
At lower temperatures, the gradient structure will minimize wear through barrier effects.
At higher temperatures, self-healing will sustain a protective lubricious film and mitigate adhesive and oxidative wear.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated specimens will have a statistically lower steady-state coefficient of friction throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated specimens will have a statistically lower specific wear rate throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has variable friction and increased wear because it cannot sustain a stable lubricious surface film.
The coating is expected to remain effective from room temperature to 800 °C under moderate-to-high sliding loads in oxidative environments.
Performance in non-oxidative atmospheres and under extreme loads remains unverified.
The coating composition, gradient profile, and processing parameters needed for optimum wide-temperature performance are not yet determined.
Oxidation can form an oxide film that lubricates the interface, reduces shear strength, and lowers friction.
